Noirlac
nwahr-LAHK
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Berry, central France, founded 1136 as a daughter of Clairvaux)
French noir, black, and lac, a lake: the black lake, from the marshy ground beside the Cher that the monks drained.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Noirlac was founded in 1136 beside the river Cher in Berry, a daughter of Clairvaux settled under Bernard's own direction, and it survives as one of the most complete Cistercian complexes in France — church, cloister, chapter house, refectory and dormitory all standing. Its later history is the one worth telling. Suppressed at the Revolution, the abbey was sold and spent the nineteenth century as a porcelain factory, with kilns in the nave and workers' families housed in the monks' range, before the state bought it back in 1909. A building raised for the praise of God spent a hundred years making china. It is hard to read that without hearing “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2), spoken of a far greater sanctuary; and “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) is the standing comment on every consecrated stone. Noirlac's stones outlasted its religion by a century and a half, which is a warning rather than a triumph.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines abbey as a monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion; and lake as a large and extensive collection of water contained in a cavity or hollow of the earth.

expand to see more

ABBEY, n. A monastery or society of persons of either sex, secluded from the world and devoted to religion. The males are called monks, and governed by an abbot; the females are called nuns, and governed by an abbess.

LAKE, n. A large and extensive collection of water contained in a cavity or hollow of the earth.

MARSH, n. A tract of soft wet land, or a tract of land occasionally overflowed by water, or covered with water.

FACTORY, n. A house or place where factors reside; also, a building appropriated to the manufacture of goods.

SUPPRESS, v.t. To crush; to subdue; to destroy; to put an end to.

Key Scripture

Mat 24:2 — "And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down."

Psa 127:1 — "A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

Heb 12:27 — "And this word, Yet once more, signifieth the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain."

Modern Corruption

A Clairvaux daughter of 1136 whose buildings survive almost whole: suppressed at the Revolution and run as a porcelain factory for a century, its stones outlasting its religion.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that buildings are not the church and cannot be made to be. “the removing of those things that are shaken, as of things that are made, that those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Heb 12:27) sorts the two categories, and a nave full of kilns is a blunt illustration of which side masonry falls on.

The live warning is complacency about endowment. Noirlac was wealthy, well built and perfectly regular, and none of that preserved a living faith in it. “except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Psa 127:1) applies to institutions that have everything except the thing they were founded for — and most of them do not notice until the kilns arrive.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

French noir lac, black lake; Hebrew bayith (H1004), a house; Hebrew eben (H68), a stone; Greek oikos (G3624), a house; Greek lithos (G3037), a stone.

expand to see more

French noir lac — the black lake; the marsh the monks drained to build.

Hebrew bayith (H1004) — a house, and so a household and a dynasty; “Except the LORD build the house” (Psa 127:1).

Hebrew eben (H68) — a stone; the material of altars, memorials and temples alike.

Greek lithos (G3037) — a stone; “There shall not be left here one stone upon another” (Mat 24:2).

Greek oikodomeo (G3618) — to build; used in the New Testament far more of people than of buildings.

Usage

"“they labour in vain that build it” (Psa 127:1) — the verdict on a house raised without God."

"“that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2) — said of the temple, and true of every abbey."

"“those things which cannot be shaken may remain” (Heb 12:27) — the sorting that outlasts masonry."
